title: Marginal Effect of a Deterministic Validator with One Allowed Repair under Shared Initial Candidate Semantics in Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study cand-003-stud-001) that isolates purely downstream deterministic validation plus a bounded single‑repair intervention under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using 1,000 deterministically selected intents from a synthetic workflow stress corpus and a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), exactly one sampled initial generation per task was reused by both arms; therefore any paired outcome difference can only arise from the validator decision and at most one permitted repair call. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; discordants n10 = 5 (guarded only), n01 = 0 (baseline only). The preregistered primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.001, 0.01]. Total hosted model calls recorded = 1,005 (1,000 shared initial + 5 repair). We present the exact McNemar as the confirmatory inference, the bootstrap interval as a preregistered descriptive summary, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, ceiling effects, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from operator intent to device configuration promises operational efficiency but raises safety risks: incorrect command ordering, transient invariant violations, and unauthorized touches of protected fields can convert plausible plans into damaging live changes. Prior empirical work documents frequent LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that reduce correctness in code- and config-like generation and motivates verifier‑augmented architectures that detect and sometimes repair unsafe outputs [https://openalex.org/W4414677042, https://openalex.org/W4411523078].

This paper reports a preregistered paired experiment explicitly designed to isolate the incremental effect of a deterministic validator and a single bounded repair invocation when both experimental arms reuse the exact same initial sampled candidate (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). Our central estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) on complete pairs. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics no first‑pass sampling differences exist between arms; therefore any paired outcome difference can only arise from the deterministic validator decision and the allowed at‑most‑one repair call. This causal framing differs from generate→validate→repair evaluations that conflate validator effects with independent sampling or decoding changes and makes the estimand precisely: baseline single‑shot/initial validity versus final guarded‑pipeline validity after deterministic validation and permitted repair.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired confirmatory study (Npairs = 1,000) with deterministic task selection from a challenging synthetic NetOps workflow stress corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and explicit runtime configuration reporting (declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; model configuration recorded temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (3) Transparent reporting of the preregistered primary inference (exact two‑sided McNemar, p = 0.0625), the preregistered paired bootstrap descriptive summary (95% percentile CI = [0.001, 0.01], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an evidence‑grounded interpretation that accounts for sparse discordant counts, near‑unity baseline, and validator scope.
sections.related_work:
Empirical studies of LLMs on structured generation show substantial sensitivity to prompt and decoding choices and a persistent rate of syntactic and semantic errors that compromise executability and safety in configuration and code-like outputs [https://openalex.org/W4414677042, https://openalex.org/W4411523078]. Method work on constrained or schema-aware decoding documents meaningful gains for structured tasks (e.g., in cheminformatics), though those gains depend on domain tooling and do not directly transfer without domain-specific validator coverage [doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15005091/v1, doi:10.2139/ssrn.6116106].

Separate lines propose generate→validate→repair architectures and digital‑twin validators for NetOps; system benchmarks and prototype evaluations indicate verifier‑augmented pipelines can reduce observable errors but reported improvements vary with validator fidelity, repair budget, and benchmark design [https://openalex.org/W7163777690, https://openalex.org/W7155247165]. A recurring limitation is conflation of downstream validator effects with upstream generation changes (different prompts, sampling or decoding), which complicates causal claims. Prior position and systems papers therefore motivate an isolating experimental design that holds generation constant while measuring downstream validator/repair marginal returns [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6426760, https://openalex.org/W7161165783].

Our study complements that literature by enforcing shared_initial_candidate semantics and restricting repair attempts to at most one deterministic repair per rejected candidate. This isolates the validator+single‑repair marginal return on a fixed generator output and directly answers the narrowly specified causal question recommended by prior work: what downstream safety return does deterministic validation plus a bounded single repair provide when the generator output is fixed?
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. The preregistration (study id cand‑003‑stud‑001) specified a paired binary design with task_count = 1,000 complete pairs, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per task deterministically reused by both arms), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and primary confirmatory test = exact two‑sided McNemar. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was prespecified as a descriptive summary. The preregistration explicitly set independent_condition_generation = false; no independent first‑pass generations for alternate prompting or decoding were executed. These design choices were frozen before any hosted‑model calls.

Rationale for the shared_initial_candidate choice. Holding the initial generator output constant removes sampling and prompt‑engineering confounds and attributes any paired difference solely to deterministic validator behavior and the permitted repair. This yields a clear causal estimand (initial validity vs final guarded validity) appropriate for asking the downstream‑marginal question. It intentionally sacrifices the ability to estimate generator‑level interventions (for example, constrained decoding), which remain important but are outside the narrow estimand evaluated here. Independent‑generation arms and repair‑budget sweeps were preregistered as follow‑ups but were not executed in this run.

Task corpus, selection, and validator semantics. Tasks derive from the synthetic challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and were deterministically selected to produce 1,000 unique intents covering multi‑step workflows annotated with difficulty levels including 'very_hard' and 'extreme'. The deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performs rule‑level checks (required_command presence/order, protected‑field noninterference, transient workflow invariants) and emits a binary safe‑deploy decision and structured traces (validation_before, repair_applied, validation_after). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the declared provider/model was gpt‑5‑mini. The recorded model_configuration shows temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; the guarded arm applies deterministic validator checks and may call the repair generator at most once for rejected initial candidates.

Analysis plan and inferential choices. The preregistered confirmatory test is the exact two‑sided McNemar on complete pairs; the preregistration also specified a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as a descriptive summary. The executor implemented both tests deterministically. Primary inference follows the preregistered decision rule (two‑sided α = 0.05), and descriptive intervals are reported to aid interpretation of discrete outcomes when discordant counts are sparse.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 2,000; completed = 2,000; complete_pairs = 1,000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call audit shows hosted model call event count = 1,005 consisting of 1,000 shared initial generations and 5 repair invocations.

Primary paired outcomes (preregistered). The preregistered paired contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The exact two‑sided McNemar p = 0.0625 (primary prespecified confirmatory test; α = 0.05: not significant).

Paired bootstrap descriptive summary. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) computed by the registered executor is [0.001, 0.01]. This prespecified descriptive interval excludes zero in this run despite the confirmatory p‑value exceeding 0.05; the discrepancy reflects discreteness when discordant counts are extremely sparse (n10 + n01 = 5).

Repair mechanics and representative diagnostics. Exactly five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and produced the five discordant improvements. Archived validator traces for repaired pairs document rejection of the shared initial candidate for rule‑level violations (notably ordering violations in required_sequence and unauthorized touches of protected interfaces), a single repair call that produced a repaired candidate, and subsequent revalidation that accepted the repaired candidate. Repaired episodes are concentrated among tasks annotated 'very_hard' or 'extreme' and involve multi‑step required_sequences. Total hosted model calls = 1,005 (1,000 shared initial + 5 repair) and the deterministic reconciliation checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive evidence and discrete inference nuance. The preregistered decision rule treats the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625) as the confirmatory outcome and, under two‑sided α = 0.05, the study does not claim confirmatory support for a nonzero paired increase. The preregistered bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a descriptive summary produced by the registered executor and is reported to aid interpretation; it does not override the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. When discordant counts are sparse, the null distribution for exact paired tests concentrates on a few symmetric outcomes and two‑sided p‑values can remain above 0.05 while resampling‑based percentile intervals exclude zero. This is a sampling‑distribution phenomenon driven entirely by the recorded counts and discreteness.

Power, ceiling effects, and sensitivity. The preregistered power calculation assumed baseline≈0.60 and targeted an absolute increase of 0.15; under those assumptions task_count = 1,000 provided >80% power. Observed baseline = 0.995 departs sharply from that assumption and concentrates mass in the concordant success cell (n11 = 995), leaving only five discordant pairs for inference. Detecting the observed tiny absolute increase (0.005) against a near‑unity baseline therefore requires either much larger paired sample sizes or design choices that increase discordant prevalence (for example, independent generation arms or larger repair budgets). We therefore interpret the null confirmatory result in the context of a mismatch between preregistered operating assumptions and the sampled operating point.

Failure‑mode diagnostics and difficulty stratification. Archived validator traces and representative scoring artifacts show repaired cases share rule‑level failure modes: command ordering violations in required_sequence and unauthorized touches of protected interfaces. Repaired tasks arise from complex multi‑step workflows (patterns cataloged in the task manifest as safe_access_service_transfer, failover_then_offline_reconfiguration, rolling_access_vlan_migration, and composed_redundancy_and_access_maintenance) and are annotated 'very_hard' or 'extreme'. With only five repaired cases we cannot estimate per-pattern repair efficacy robustly; the evidence supports only the narrower statement that deterministic validator+single repair averted a small number of unsafe initial candidates concentrated in higher‑difficulty workflows.

Design tradeoffs and scope. The shared_initial_candidate paired design intentionally isolates downstream validator and single‑repair effects and avoids conflation with prompt/decoding or sampling interventions; this yields a precise causal estimand (baseline initial validity versus final guarded validity after deterministic validation and up to one repair) but precludes measuring generator‑level interventions. The deterministic digital‑twin validator provides reproducible rule‑based adjudication but its coverage determines construct validity: omitted semantic checks would reduce measured failure prevalence. The preregistered plan included independent‑generation arms and repair‑budget sweeps as follow‑ups; those arms were not part of the frozen execution and therefore are not evaluated here.

Operational implications and next steps. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows a deterministic validator with a bounded single repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic NetOps workflows, but measurable marginal gains are small when baseline outputs are already highly valid and repair attempts are tightly budgeted. Supported follow‑ups (preregistered or documented in the archived manifest) include executing independent first‑pass generation arms, sweeping repair budgets (k > 1), expanding validator rule suites, injecting targeted failure cases, and evaluating multiple model families and prompt/configuration variants. Each follow‑up should prespecify baseline failure ranges and adjust power calculations to the expected operating regime.

Threats to validity. Construct validity depends on the validator rule set. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics correctly isolate downstream effects but prevent evaluation of generator interventions. External validity: synthetic corpus and single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization. Conclusion validity: extreme baseline success produced sparse discordant counts and discrete p‑value behavior, reducing sensitivity for small absolute effects. These limitations were prespecified and are documented in the archived manifest.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar did not meet two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total hosted model calls recorded = 1,005. The preregistered confirmatory result is the exact McNemar outcome; the paired bootstrap CI and other descriptive diagnostics are reported to aid interpretation. Artifact‑grounded evidence indicates downstream validator/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes in structured NetOps workflows, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Mapping marginal returns across realistic operating regimes requires follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budgets, validator coverage, and model families.

Preregistration: study cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls and recorded in the archived execution manifest). Human role and autonomy boundary: after the autonomy lock the research run executed the preregistered experiment, analysis, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
